stem: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
options: Yawning brings extra oxygen to a tired brain, which is why people yawn when they are sleepy.
Scientists have proposed several explanations for yawning, but none has been proven.
Contagious yawning proves that people feel more empathy for strangers than for family members.
Dogs, cats, and fish yawn just as often as humans do, which shows that yawning is very old.
explanation: A summary covers the main idea of the whole passage: several theories, none proven.
distractors: A: the passage says this idea "did not hold up." C: reverses the detail (people catch yawns more from family) and overstates it as proof. D: the passage says animals yawn but never compares how often or discusses age.

stem: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
options: Oysters help clean the bay's water, and people are working to restore them.
A single adult oyster can filter as much as 50 gallons of water in just one day.
Overharvesting was the only reason the bay's oyster population fell sharply.
Underwater grasses in the bay give shelter to young crabs and many kinds of fish.
explanation: The best summary covers the oysters' main role (filtering water) and the effort to restore them; the other options are single details or misstatements.
distractors: B: a single detail, not the main idea. C: the passage also names disease and pollution. D: a supporting detail, not the main idea.

stem: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
options: Nightingale helped establish a nursing school at St Thomas' Hospital in London in 1860.
Most soldiers who died in the Crimean War were killed by their wounds from battle.
Nightingale's statistics showed most deaths were preventable and helped bring about reforms.
Nightingale's book Notes on Nursing taught nurses how to draw statistical charts.
explanation: The passage's main point is that Nightingale used careful records and statistics to show that most deaths came from preventable disease, which helped change policy.
distractors: A: a single detail from the last paragraph. B: contradicts the passage: most died of disease. D: the passage says the book stressed fresh air, clean water, and cleanliness.

stem: Which sentence best summarizes the story?
options: A charge nurse hands Dana a clipboard and a list of eight residents to care for.
On her first day, Dana asks why a resident won't eat, gets his problem fixed, and earns praise.
A resident refuses his lunch because he dislikes the food that the kitchen serves him every day.
Dana arrives early but decides by the end of the day that the job is too hard.
explanation: A summary of a story covers its beginning, key event, and outcome.
distractors: A: a detail from the opening, not the whole story. C: gives the wrong reason; his dentures hurt. D: contradicts the ending: she looks forward to tomorrow.

stem: What can the reader infer from Ms. Okafor's comment at the end of the story?
options: She values staff who pay close attention to residents' needs.
She is upset that Dana spent so long talking with Mr. Bell.
She plans to promote Dana to charge nurse right away.
She thinks Dana should have called the kitchen herself.
explanation: She praises Dana for noticing something others missed and calls that what the job is "really about."
distractors: B: her words are praise, not criticism. C: nothing in the story suggests a promotion. D: Ms. Okafor called the kitchen and doesn't criticize Dana for reporting it.

stem: According to the brain-cooling explanation, in which situation would a person be LEAST likely to yawn?
options: Watching a family member yawn
Reading an article about yawning
Sitting in a cool room after a long day
Standing outside on a very hot day
explanation: The passage says people yawn less when the outside air is very hot, because a deep breath wouldn't cool anything.
distractors: A: contagious yawning would make a yawn more likely. B: the passage says reading about yawns can trigger one. C: cool air would make a cooling yawn useful.

stem: A student parks on campus on January 20 without a spring permit. What will most likely happen?
options: The student will receive a warning notice.
The student will receive a $25 ticket.
The student's car will be towed away.
Nothing will happen, because permits are free.
explanation: From January 12 to January 26, vehicles without a permit get a warning; tickets start after January 26.
distractors: B: tickets start after January 26. C: the memo never mentions towing. D: permits being free doesn't mean they're optional.

stem: In Story B, why does Mr. Lyle most likely keep planting tomatoes along the fence?
options: He does not know where the sunny corner of the yard is.
His neighbor told him that the fence was the best place in the yard to plant tomatoes.
He is attached to the way things were done when his wife was alive.
He believes tomatoes grow best in the shade.
explanation: His grumbling that tomatoes grew there "when his wife was alive" suggests habit and memory, not reasons about sunlight.
distractors: A: he moves the plants there easily once he decides to. B: the neighbor suggested the fence was the problem. D: the story never says this; he says tomatoes "had always grown there."

stem: A patient with an 8:00 a.m. fasting test eats a granola bar at 9:30 p.m. the night before. According to the directions, what should the patient do?
options: Go to the test as planned without mentioning the snack.
Arrive two hours late so that the fast lasts longer.
Drink extra water to wash out the food before the test.
Call the lab, because the test may need to be rescheduled.
explanation: The last line says: "If you eat by mistake during the fasting period, call the lab. You may need to reschedule."
distractors: A: the directions say to call the lab if you eat by mistake. B: the directions don't offer this option. C: water is allowed, but it doesn't undo eating.

stem: According to the label, what should a parent do before giving these tablets to an 8-year-old with hay fever?
options: Give 1 tablet every 24 hours.
Ask a doctor.
Give half a tablet every 24 hours.
Never use the product for this child.
explanation: For children 6 to under 12 years, the label says "ask a doctor."
distractors: A: that dose is for ages 12 and over. C: the label gives no half-tablet dose. D: "Do not use" applies to children under 6.

stem: A person follows the saline-rinse directions but swallows the water after gargling. Which instruction did the person fail to follow?
options: Stir until the salt dissolves.
Make a fresh mixture each time.
Spit the water into the sink.
Wash your hands first.
explanation: The directions say: "Spit the water into the sink; do not swallow it."
distractors: A: has nothing to do with swallowing. B: has nothing to do with swallowing. D: has nothing to do with swallowing.

stem: According to the memo, where can students pick up their parking permits?
options: At the visitor spaces near the main entrance
On the student portal
At the campus bookstore
Room 104 in the Workforce Building
explanation: Permits are picked up at the Campus Safety office, Room 104, Workforce Building.
distractors: A: that's where visitors park. B: the portal is where you fill out the form, not where you pick up the permit. C: the memo doesn't mention a bookstore.

stem: According to the passage, in what year did Nightingale publish Notes on Nursing?
explanation: The passage says, "In 1859 she published Notes on Nursing."
distractors: A: the year she arrived at Scutari. B: a year the passage doesn't mention. D: the year the nursing school was established.

stem: According to the label, at what temperature should the tablets be stored?
explanation: The label says to store the tablets at 68–77 °F.
distractors: A: much colder than the label's range. B: cooler than the label's range. D: warmer than the label's range.

stem: A patient wants a blood draw and a dental cleaning on the same day. On which days is that possible?
options: Monday or Wednesday
Tuesday or Thursday
Wednesday or Friday
Monday or Friday
explanation: Dental cleanings run only on Tuesday and Thursday, and the lab is open both of those mornings.
distractors: A: dental is closed on both days, and the lab is closed on Wednesday. C: the lab is closed on Wednesday, and dental is closed on both days. D: dental cleanings are closed on Monday and Friday.

stem: Which age groups met the health department's goal?
options: Only adults 65 and older
Adults 50–64 and adults 65 and older
None of the age groups
All groups over age 30
explanation: Only the 65+ group (71%) reached at least 70%.
distractors: B: 50–64 reached only 52%. C: the 65+ group reached 71%, which meets the 70% goal. D: 30–49 reached only 35%.

stem: According to the survey, how many more minutes did students who used screens for more than 60 minutes before bed take to fall asleep than students who used no screens?
options: 11 minutes
15 minutes
26 minutes
41 minutes
explanation: 41 minutes − 15 minutes = 26 minutes.
distractors: A: 41 − 30 = 11; this subtracts a screen-time category boundary (30 minutes) instead of the no-screen group's 15 minutes. B: this is the time for the no-screens group. D: this is the total time for the more-than-60-minutes group, not the difference.

stem: Which of these events happened first?
options: Nightingale published Notes on Nursing.
Nightingale helped establish a nursing school in London.
Nightingale worked with statisticians on death rates.
Nightingale arrived at the army hospital in Scutari.
explanation: She arrived in 1854, during the war; the analysis, book, and school all came later.
distractors: A: 1859, after the war. B: 1860, the last event in the passage. C: this happened after the war.

stem: What happened immediately after Mr. Bell explained that his dentures hurt?
options: Dana reported the problem to Ms. Okafor.
Ms. Okafor called the kitchen.
Mr. Bell ate every bite of his meal.
Dana recorded every meal in the chart.
explanation: The order is: Mr. Bell explains → Dana reports → Ms. Okafor calls the kitchen → the soup arrives → he eats.
distractors: B: this happened after Dana reported the problem. C: this happened later, after the soup arrived. D: this happened earlier in the morning.

stem: Put these steps for making the saline rinse in the correct order.
options: Stir in one-half teaspoon of salt.
Wash your hands.
Gargle for about 30 seconds.
Pour warm water into a clean glass.
explanation: The directions say first wash your hands, next pour warm water, then add salt and stir, and then gargle.
distractors: Common error: adding salt before the water is in the glass. Another: gargling before the salt dissolves.

stem: Which sentence from the letter states an opinion?
options: A 20-ounce bottle of regular soda contains about 16 teaspoons of sugar.
Several hospitals across the country have already stopped selling sugary drinks.
Last week I visited my father at Bayside General Hospital.
Nothing could be more ridiculous.
explanation: "Ridiculous" expresses a judgment that can't be proven true or false.
distractors: A: a measurable fact. B: a fact that could be checked. C: a fact about the writer's experience.

stem: Which statement in the advertisement is a fact that could be checked?
options: Each gummy contains 3 mg of melatonin.
DreamDeep is the most amazing sleep aid ever made.
Ordinary sleeping pills are harsh.
"I haven't slept this well in years!"
explanation: The amount of an ingredient can be measured and verified.
distractors: B: opinion and exaggeration. C: "harsh" is a judgment word, not a measurable fact. D: one customer's personal opinion, which can't be checked.

stem: Which misconception does the advertisement encourage?
options: That melatonin is a hormone that plays a role in sleep cycles
That sleeping pills require a prescription
That berry flavors make gummies taste better
That a product labeled natural must be safe for everyone
explanation: The ad says the product is "100% natural, so it is completely safe for everyone." Natural substances can still have side effects and interactions.
distractors: A: this is true, not a misconception, and the ad never mentions it. B: the ad never says this. C: the ad doesn't argue this.

stem: Which statement from the letter best shows the writer's bias?
options: A 20-ounce bottle of regular soda contains about 16 teaspoons of sugar.
Every hospital administrator who keeps these machines stocked is simply putting profit ahead of patients.
The American Heart Association recommends that most women limit added sugar to about 6 teaspoons a day and most men to about 9.
Several hospitals across the country have already stopped selling sugary drinks.
explanation: Saying that "every" administrator acts only for profit is an overgeneralization that assumes motives without evidence.
distractors: A: a factual statement. C: a factual statement attributed to a named health organization. D: a factual statement.

stem: Which statement from the passages is a fact rather than an opinion?
options: Starting high school at 8:30 a.m. or later is a simple change that protects students' health.
Later start times sound good, but the details matter.
During puberty, the brain begins releasing the sleep hormone melatonin later at night.
Before changing the schedule, our district should study what the change would cost.
explanation: The timing of melatonin release is a scientific finding that can be checked.
distractors: A: "simple" and the recommendation are judgments. B: a judgment. D: "should" signals a recommendation, not a fact.

stem: In the last paragraph, the word humble in "the humble yawn" most nearly means
options: ordinary
proud
dangerous
mysterious
explanation: The author contrasts an everyday, ordinary act with the fact that it is still a mystery.
distractors: B: the opposite meaning. C: nothing in the passage suggests danger. D: the sentence calls the yawn a mystery, but "humble" describes how ordinary it is.

stem: In the last sentence, the word promising most nearly means
options: guaranteed to work
likely to succeed
very expensive
recently discovered
explanation: Scientists see restoration as a way that will likely improve the bay's health.
distractors: A: too strong; the passage says restoration takes time. C: the passage doesn't discuss cost. D: the passage says restoration takes time and has gone on for years; "promising" isn't about newness.

stem: In the first sentence, the word pioneer most nearly means
options: one of the first people to do something
a soldier who fought in a war
a person who criticizes the government
a teacher at a nursing school
explanation: Nightingale was among the first to use statistics to change policy.
distractors: B: she was a nurse, not a soldier. C: the passage describes her persuading officials, not criticizing them. D: she helped establish a school, but "pioneer" refers to being first.

stem: In the first paragraph, the word luxury most nearly means
options: a requirement that every student must meet before graduating
something nice to have but not necessary
a costly mistake that a college later regrets making
a special reward given to students for high grades
explanation: The author says online tutoring is "not a luxury" but a necessity, so luxury means something extra.
distractors: A: the opposite: the author contrasts luxury with necessity. C: the sentence isn't about mistakes. D: the sentence isn't about rewards.

stem: On the label, the word temporarily in "temporarily relieves sneezing" most nearly means
options: for all time
in every way
for a limited time
at a slow pace
explanation: The tablets relieve symptoms for a while, which is why a dose is taken every 24 hours.
distractors: A: the opposite meaning. B: describes how much, not how long. D: describes speed, not how long.

stem: Why does the author most likely end the passage with the question in parentheses?
options: To prove that the brain-cooling explanation is correct
To warn readers that frequent yawning is a sign of illness
To playfully show that reading about yawns can cause one
To introduce a new theory that will be explained next
explanation: The question connects to the earlier point that reading about yawns can trigger one, in a light, friendly way.
distractors: A: the passage says none of the explanations is proven. B: the passage never discusses illness. D: it's the last sentence; nothing follows.

stem: What is the main purpose of the advertisement?
options: To explain the science of how melatonin works
To persuade readers to buy the product
To entertain readers with a story about sleep
To compare several sleep aids fairly
explanation: Superlatives, testimonials, and "Order today" show that the goal is to sell.
distractors: A: the ad gives almost no science. C: there's no story. D: it compares only to "harsh sleeping pills," and not fairly.

stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To tell patients how to prepare for a fasting blood test
To persuade patients that they should get blood tests more often
To explain how labs analyze blood samples
To describe the history of fasting
explanation: Numbered steps and commands such as "Stop eating" show that the purpose is to instruct.
distractors: B: it doesn't argue for more tests. C: it doesn't describe lab work. D: it includes no history.

stem: Why does the author mention underwater grasses in the second paragraph?
options: To explain why oysters became less common
To argue that grasses filter more water than oysters do
To describe what oysters eat as they filter the water
To show how oysters help other living things
explanation: Clearer water lets light reach the grasses, which shelter crabs and fish: a chain of benefits.
distractors: A: the decline is discussed in the third paragraph. B: the passage never compares the two. C: the passage says oysters trap algae and sediment; the grasses are mentioned as shelter, not food.

stem: Why does the writer include the amount of sugar in a bottle of soda?
options: To show that the writer's father drinks too much soda
To compare the prices of drinks in the hospital store
To explain how the vending machine works
To support the claim that sugary drinks are unhealthy
explanation: Comparing 16 teaspoons with the recommended daily limits backs up the argument with evidence.
distractors: A: the letter doesn't say what the father drinks. B: no prices are given. C: the letter never describes how the machine works.

stem: The author of Passage B is a parent and bus company owner. How does this background most likely shape the author's view?
options: The author focuses on how teenagers' bodies respond to sleep loss.
The author focuses on how later start times affect lesson plans.
The author focuses on buses, costs, and family schedules.
The author focuses on students' wish to sleep later in the morning.
explanation: The author's concerns (buses in shifts, the cost of drivers, and after-school schedules) match a parent's and bus owner's experience.
distractors: A: this is Passage A's focus. B: Passage B never mentions lessons or teaching. D: Passage B doesn't discuss what students want.

stem: The author of Passage A would most likely agree with which statement?
options: School schedules should be adjusted to fit teenagers' biology.
Teenagers who sleep late are simply lazy.
The cost of extra buses matters more than students' health and safety.
Start times have no effect on attendance.
explanation: Passage A argues that teen body clocks shift later, so schools should start later.
distractors: B: Passage A says "Teenagers are not lazy." C: Passage A puts students' health and safety first; neither passage says bus costs matter more than safety. D: Passage A cites better attendance after later starts.

stem: Which best describes the author's point of view toward around-the-clock online tutoring?
options: Neutral
Strongly opposed
Unsure
Strongly in favor
explanation: The author calls it "the difference between getting help and getting none" and answers critics.
distractors: A: the author takes a clear side. B: the author argues for it. C: the author states the position firmly.

stem: From which point of view is the story told?
options: First person, by Dana
First person, by Mr. Bell
Third person, by a narrator who follows Dana
Second person, addressing the reader as "you"
explanation: The narrator uses "Dana" and "she" and stays close to Dana's experience.
distractors: A: the story says "Dana," "she," and "her," not "I." B: Mr. Bell is described from the outside. D: the story doesn't address the reader.

stem: Which word best describes the writer's attitude toward the vending machines in the hospital lobby?
options: amused
disapproving
indifferent
admiring
explanation: The writer calls the setup "ridiculous" and demands that the drinks be removed.
distractors: A: the writer is critical, not entertained. C: the writer clearly cares. D: the opposite attitude.

stem: If restoration adds many oysters to a river, what would most likely happen over time?
options: The water would become cloudier as the growing oysters stirred up mud from the bottom.
Crabs and fish would leave because the reef took their space.
The water would become clearer, and underwater grasses would increase.
The oysters would reach market size within a few months.
explanation: More oysters filter more water; clearer water lets sunlight reach the grasses.
distractors: A: the passage says fewer oysters led to cloudier water. B: the passage says reefs shelter small animals. D: the passage says it takes about two to three years.

stem: Based on both sources, what should a student who wants to fall asleep faster most likely do?
options: Stop using screens an hour before bed and read a paper book instead.
Use a phone in bed but turn the screen brightness all the way up.
Watch videos until feeling sleepy and then put the phone away.
Exercise hard right before bed to get tired.
explanation: The article recommends no screens for an hour before bed, and the survey shows the no-screen group fell asleep fastest.
distractors: B: brighter light would make the problem worse. C: the survey links more screen time with taking longer to fall asleep. D: neither source discusses exercise.

stem: Based on Story A, what would Marisol most likely do if one of her later designs failed?
options: Give up on building contests altogether.
Blame the judges for setting the weights unfairly.
Build the same design again and hope for better luck.
Study why it failed and change the design.
explanation: After her first failure, she studied the broken pieces and improved the joints, a pattern she would likely repeat.
distractors: A: she kept trying after her first failure. B: she looked for the cause in her own design. C: she changed the design after studying the breaks.

stem: Which lines from the directions best support the conclusion that a patient's activities before the test can affect its accuracy?
options: Schedule your blood draw for the morning if you can. Most of your fasting time will then happen while you sleep.
Take your usual medicines with water unless your provider told you to stop them.
Do not chew gum, smoke, or exercise hard during the fasting period. These can change your results.
Keep drinking plain water. Water makes your veins easier to find.
explanation: These lines say directly that these activities can change the results.
distractors: A: about convenience, not accuracy. B: about medicines, not about what can change results. D: about finding a vein, not about results.

stem: Suppose next season the vaccination rate for adults 30–49 rises by 20 percentage points. Based on the survey, would that group then meet the health department's goal?
options: Yes, because the rate would reach 70% or more.
No, because the rate would reach only 55%.
Yes, because the rate would then be higher than every other group's.
No, because the rate would fall below the 18–29 group's rate.
explanation: 35% + 20 percentage points = 55%, still short of the 70% goal.
distractors: A: 35% + 20 = 55%, which is below 70%. C: 55% would be higher than the 50–64 group's 52% but still below the 65+ group's 71%; in any case, the goal is 70%, not beating other groups. D: 55% would be above 28%; the reason is wrong.

stem: Which theme do both stories share?
options: Winning a contest matters more than enjoying the work you do.
Advice from neighbors and friends usually turns out to be wrong in the end.
Some problems can never be solved, no matter how hard you try.
Learning from failure and changing your approach can lead to success.
explanation: Both characters fail, change their approach, and then succeed.
distractors: A: only Story A has a contest, and it isn't the message. B: the neighbor's advice in Story B turns out to be right. C: both characters solve their problems.

stem: How does Mr. Lyle's response to failure differ from Marisol's?
options: Marisol gives up on contests, while Mr. Lyle keeps planting in the same spot.
Marisol finds the problem on her own, while Mr. Lyle at first resists advice.
Mr. Lyle studies the problem on his own, while Marisol waits for advice.
Both characters succeed on the first try without changing anything.
explanation: Marisol studies the breaks right away; Mr. Lyle ignores his neighbor for a season before he changes.
distractors: A: Marisol doesn't give up. C: this reverses the characters. D: both fail first.

stem: How do the two passages differ in focus?
options: Passage A focuses on student health; Passage B focuses on costs and logistics.
Passage A focuses on bus schedules, while Passage B focuses on sleep hormones.
Both passages focus mainly on how later start times affect after-school sports.
Passage A opposes later start times, while Passage B strongly supports them.
explanation: A discusses body clocks, sleep, and safety; B discusses buses, costs, and schedules.
distractors: B: this reverses the passages. C: only Passage B mentions sports, briefly. D: Passage A supports them; B urges caution.

stem: On which point would both authors most likely agree?
options: Later start times should begin immediately in every district.
The cost of more buses is not worth considering.
Teenagers need less sleep than younger children.
Students' well-being matters when schools set their schedules.
explanation: A argues for teen health; B worries about young children at bus stops in the dark and about students' jobs. Both care about students.
distractors: A: Passage B wants the change studied first. B: Passage B says cost is a major concern. C: neither passage compares how much sleep teens and younger children need.

stem: Which theme is shared by "First Shift" and Story A ("The Bridge")?
options: Hard work always leads to a promotion.
It is best to follow the same routine every day, even when it isn't working.
Paying close attention to details helps solve problems.
Winning is the most important goal.
explanation: Dana notices why Mr. Bell won't eat; Marisol notices where her bridge broke. Careful observation solves each problem.
distractors: A: neither story involves a promotion. B: both characters succeed by noticing something new. D: "First Shift" has no competition.

stem: Which evidence does the author use to support the claim that online tutoring helps students succeed?
options: Community college students juggle classes with jobs, families, and long commutes.
The campus tutoring center closes long before many working students are able to study.
Good tutoring services train their tutors to ask guiding questions instead of giving answers.
Students who used online tutoring at least three times were more likely to pass their math course.
explanation: The pass-rate finding directly links using tutoring to better outcomes.
distractors: A: describes students' lives, not the results of tutoring. B: explains the need, not the effect. C: answers a critic; it isn't evidence of results.

stem: How does the author respond to critics who say online tutoring is too expensive?
options: By admitting that the cost is too high and suggesting a cheaper option instead of tutoring
By arguing that failing and retaking courses costs students and colleges more
By saying that money doesn't matter in education
By ignoring the concern entirely
explanation: The author answers the counterargument with a cost comparison: "the cost of a student failing … is far higher."
distractors: A: the author doesn't concede the point. C: the author compares costs rather than dismissing them. D: the author addresses it directly.

stem: Which is the weakest part of the writer's argument?
options: The fact that a 20-ounce bottle of regular soda contains about 16 teaspoons of sugar
The example of hospitals across the country whose stores still make money after dropping sugary drinks
The claim that every administrator who keeps the machines stocked puts profit ahead of patients
The point that hospitals are supposed to protect the health of their patients
explanation: The writer assumes the motives of every administrator without evidence. It's an overgeneralization.
distractors: A: a specific fact that supports the argument. B: evidence that the change can work. D: a reasonable premise.

stem: What is the advertisement's main evidence that DreamDeep works?
options: Statements from satisfied customers
Results from a clinical trial
Approval by the Food and Drug Administration
A recommendation from a doctor
explanation: The ad relies on testimonials such as Jamie's, which are weak evidence.
distractors: B: the ad cites no study. C: the fine print says the FDA has not evaluated these statements. D: no doctor is quoted.

stem: Which additional evidence would most strengthen Passage B's argument?
options: A study showing that teenagers' bodies release melatonin later at night than adults' do
A cost estimate showing how many extra buses and drivers the change would require
A survey showing that most high school students would prefer to sleep later
A list of the school districts that have already moved to later start times
explanation: Passage B's main concern is cost, so specific cost figures would support it best.
distractors: A: supports Passage A, not B. C: supports later start times. D: doesn't address cost.

stem: How does the survey in Source 2 relate to the article in Source 1?
options: It shows that screen time before bed has no effect on how long students take to fall asleep.
Its results fit the article's advice: more screen time before bed goes with less sleep.
It proves that blue light causes sleep problems.
It contradicts the article by showing that screens help students sleep.
explanation: Students with more screen time before bed fell asleep more slowly and slept less, which fits the article's advice.
distractors: A: times rise from 15 to 41 minutes as screen use increases. C: the survey doesn't measure blue light, and it can't prove a cause. D: the data show the opposite.

stem: Source 1 says screens delay the release of melatonin. Why can't the survey in Source 2, by itself, show that screen use causes students to sleep less?
options: It shows a pattern, but other factors could affect both screen use and sleep.
It shows that students who used no screens slept the least of any group.
It found no clear pattern between screen use and average hours of sleep.
It does not report any averages for the students who took part in it.
explanation: A survey shows things happening together (a correlation). Other factors, such as stress or late-night jobs, could explain both, so the survey alone can't prove cause. The article's explanation is what suggests a cause.
distractors: B: the no-screen group slept the most (7.4 hours). C: sleep falls steadily from 7.4 to 6.2 hours as screen use rises. D: the table reports average minutes and hours.

stem: A patient needs the fasting blood test described in the directions and wants to go to Shore Health Clinic. Which plan follows both the directions and the clinic's hours?
options: Stop eating at 9 p.m. Tuesday and get the blood draw at 9 a.m. Wednesday.
Stop eating at 11 p.m. Wednesday and get the blood draw at 7 a.m. Thursday.
Stop eating at 7 p.m. Friday and get the blood draw at 7 a.m. Saturday.
Stop eating at 7 p.m. Wednesday and get the blood draw at 7 a.m. Thursday.
explanation: 7 p.m. to 7 a.m. is 12 hours, and the lab is open Thursday from 7 to 11 a.m.
distractors: A: the lab is closed on Wednesday. B: only 8 hours of fasting; the directions require 12. C: the clinic is closed on Saturday.

stem: Which statement is supported by the survey data?
options: Most adults aged 30–49 got a flu shot.
Every age group met the 70% goal.
Vaccination rates were higher in each older age group.
Adults 50–64 were vaccinated at twice the rate of adults 65 and older.
explanation: The rates rise steadily: 28%, 35%, 52%, 71%.
distractors: A: only 35% did. B: only the 65+ group did. D: 52% is lower than 71%.

stem: A shopper compares the Allergy Relief label with the DreamDeep advertisement. Which difference between the two texts matters most for using a product safely?
options: Both texts list the same side effects and warn against drinking alcohol.
The ad gives a dose for each age group, while the label gives no dose at all.
The label lists warnings and limits on use, while the ad claims the product is safe for everyone.
The label says its product is all natural, while the ad lists only chemical ingredients and side effects.
explanation: The label tells users when not to take the product and what to watch for; the ad's "completely safe for everyone" claim gives no such guidance.
distractors: A: only the label gives warnings; the ad lists none. B: this reverses the texts: the label gives doses by age. D: the ad, not the label, claims to be natural.
